Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: try hard not think about the trauma
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

I should have protected others and I failed

issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Amir had been a paramedic for fifteen years, a man who believed he could function in the eye of any storm. That belief shattered six months ago on a rain-slicked stretch of the I-5. He was off-duty, driving home, when he came upon the multi-car pile-up. The flash of blue and red lights was as familiar to him as his own heartbeat, but the sight of his wife’s crumpled sedan pushed all the air from his lungs. His eight-year-old son, Omar, had been in the passenger seat. The moments that followed are a slideshow of sensory fragments for him now. He remembers the specific, sickening angle of Omar’s leg, the sight of the wound stark against his small frame. He remembers the smell, a nauseating mix of rain, gasoline, and the sterile, antiseptic odor from the first-aid kit he always kept in his car. But there are parts he cannot access, a black hole of several minutes between seeing the wreck and working on his own son in the back of the responding ambulance. No matter how hard he tries to retrieve that time, it remains blank, and trying to fill it brings on a wave of the same raw terror he felt then, a feeling of absolute, helpless freefall.

In the weeks after Omar was discharged from the hospital, a new, suffocating reality began to set in for Amir. He had come to believe that the man he was before the accident was gone forever, replaced by this hollowed-out, hyper-alert stranger. He saw himself as permanently damaged goods. At home, he found himself unable to sit still, throwing himself into tasks with a frantic energy—reorganizing the garage, fixing a fence that wasn’t broken—anything to occupy the space in his head where the memories threatened to bloom. When a memory did break through, it wasn't a simple recollection; it was a full-body hijacking. The faint smell of bleach his wife, Layla, used to clean the bathroom would suddenly become the overwhelming chemical sting of the ER, and he would be back in the ambulance, the phantom weight of his son's small body in his arms, the sirens screaming in his ears as if it were happening all over again.

His identity as a protector, both at home and at work, felt like a cruel joke. He was certain he had failed Omar in the most fundamental way, that a better father, a better paramedic, would have done something different. This conviction that he couldn't rely on himself began to seep into his professional life. He started calling in sick, avoiding shifts because the thought of the ambulance, the injuries, the very smell of the hospital, was unbearable. On the days he did force himself to go in, he was a ghost of his former self. He found his concentration shattered, unable to follow a simple briefing, his mind drifting back to the slick asphalt and broken glass. He would position himself in the station’s break room with his back to a corner, needing to see every entrance, a habit that drew quiet, concerned looks from his colleagues. The final straw at work was when a partner clapped him on the shoulder from behind to get his attention, and Amir flinched so violently he knocked a tray of supplies to the floor.

The tension followed him home. Layla’s gentle touch, once a comfort, now made him jump with alarm. The distance between them grew into a silent, painful chasm. It was after a particularly bad night, when he woke up shouting from a dream he couldn't remember, that Layla sat with him at the kitchen table and told him, her voice soft with worry, "I miss my husband. Omar misses his father. We need you back." Amir is now seeking help not because he believes he can be fixed—he is fairly certain that is impossible—but because the man he has become is a stranger to his own family. He is terrified that this broken version of himself is all that is left, but a small, desperate part of him hopes to one day be able to sit beside his son without seeing the ghost of his injuries, and to feel his wife’s touch as an act of love, not a threat.
